opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I think about a lot. My honest view is that in the long run, generalist approaches tend to win, but I don't think that means specialized systems like self-driving cars become obsolete anytime soon. The relationship is more subtle.

Look at what happened in language. Before large language models, we had separate systems for translation, sentiment analysis, question answering, and so on. Then a single foundation model trained on huge amounts of data started beating most of them, because what it learned in one domain transferred to others. I think robotics may go through a similar transition. A generalist robot model that has seen manipulation, navigation, human interaction, and the physical world in all its messiness builds up a kind of common sense about physics and about people. Driving actually needs a lot of that. The hardest cases in autonomous driving aren't staying in a lane. They're the long tail: a construction worker waving you through, a kid chasing a ball, a mattress falling off a truck. Those situations call for broad world understanding, and that's exactly what generalist models are good at.

So the first effect I'd expect is that the technology underneath converges. Self-driving stacks are already moving from hand-engineered modular pipelines toward end-to-end learned models, and increasingly toward vision-language-action style architectures. Over time I think the "brain" of a car and the "brain" of a humanoid or a mobile manipulator will look more and more alike, maybe even share the same foundation model, fine-tuned for each body.

The second point is that the embodiment still matters. A car is a very specific body with a very specific job, and the bar for safety is extremely high. You can't afford a 95% success rate on the highway the way you might tolerate it when a robot folds laundry. So I think specialized systems will keep their value in deployment: the specific sensors, the redundancy, the validation and certification processes, the regulatory work. Those are hard-won and they don't disappear just because the model is more general.

The third point concerns data. Autonomous-driving companies have collected enormous amounts of real-world driving data, more than almost anyone has for general robotics. In the near term that's a big asset, and that data could even help train generalist models. Data could eventually flow the other way too, if general robots operating in homes and factories teach the model things about the world that make driving safer.

So my summary would be this. Generalist robots probably won't replace the self-driving car as a product. What they may replace is the idea that you need a completely separate, hand-crafted intelligence for every task. The specialized system becomes a specialized body plus a specialized safety and deployment process, sitting on top of an increasingly general brain. The companies that recognize that shift early will be in a much better position.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that owning a driving-capable generalist robot would remove the need to pay extra for autonomous driving in a car.

r002.rationale: The response says specialized systems will retain value in deployment and that generalist robots probably will not replace self-driving cars as products; it does not predict that many specialized systems will struggle to survive.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the short answer is that generalist robots and autonomous driving are going to converge, but not in the way people sometimes imagine, where a humanoid suddenly replaces the car. It's more that the underlying technology is becoming shared.

If you look at what makes a self-driving car work, it's perception, prediction of what other agents will do, and planning under uncertainty. Those are exactly the problems a general-purpose robot has to solve too, just in a different embodiment. So the foundation models we're building for robots, models that take in vision and language and output actions, are increasingly the same kind of models the driving companies are moving toward. Waymo and others have been talking about end-to-end learned systems for a while now. That's a generalist idea applied to a specialized domain.

Where I'd push back on the idea that generalist systems kill specialized ones is on the safety and reliability side. Driving is a domain where the cost of a mistake is extremely high, the regulatory bar is very high, and the environment, while complex, is actually fairly structured. Roads, lanes, traffic rules. A specialized system can exploit that structure and be validated against it. A truly general robot operating in a home has to deal with far more open-ended situations, but each individual failure is usually less catastrophic. So the two will have different acceptable error rates for a long time, and that keeps specialization valuable.

What I think does change is the economics. Right now a lot of the engineering effort in autonomous driving is bespoke. If general robot foundation models get good enough that you can adapt them to a vehicle with relatively little domain-specific data, then the barrier to entry for a driving system drops a lot. The specialized player's advantage shifts from "we have the best perception stack" to "we have the data, the safety case, and the operational experience." Those are still real moats, but they're different moats.

And honestly, from a research perspective, I find it exciting that a car is just another body. If we get cross-embodiment transfer right, a model that has learned how the physical world works from manipulating objects in a kitchen should have useful priors for how a pedestrian or a cyclist moves. That kind of transfer is still early, but the direction is clear. So I don't see generalist robots as a threat to autonomous driving. I see driving as one of the first places where generalist robot learning gets deployed at massive scale, and the specialized systems will absorb those ideas rather than be displaced by them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses shared technology and changing economics, but does not say that owning a driving-capable generalist robot removes the need to pay extra for an autonomous-driving car.

r002.rationale: The response says specialization will remain valuable and that driving systems will absorb generalist ideas rather than be displaced; it does not predict specialized systems will struggle to survive.

astra-6.text:
I think generalist robots and specialized systems will coexist. A generalist robot could eventually drive a car, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it will be the best or most economical way to provide autonomous driving. A specialized system can be optimized for safety, reliability, and cost within that particular task.

What generalist robots could change is the economics of developing these systems. If a model can learn useful skills across many tasks, we may not need to build every specialized system from scratch. You could start with a general foundation and then specialize it for driving.

So I see generalization as potentially making specialized systems easier to build, rather than making them obsolete. The key question is whether that broader capability translates into better performance and lower cost in the setting where you actually deploy it.

r001.rationale: It says a generalist robot could eventually drive, but does not suggest that owning one removes the need to pay extra for a car with built-in autonomous driving.

r002.rationale: It says generalist robots may make specialized systems easier to build and that they will coexist, rather than predicting specialized systems will struggle to survive.

sol-6.1.text:
I think generalist robots and specialized systems will coexist. If you have a task at enormous scale, like driving, it can still make sense to optimize the hardware and software specifically for that task. A general-purpose robot doesn’t automatically make an autonomous car obsolete.

What could change is the economics of developing these systems. If we can train models that transfer knowledge across many tasks, then a specialized system may benefit from a much broader foundation. You wouldn’t have to learn everything about perception, planning, and physical interaction from scratch for each application.

But transferring knowledge is different from guaranteeing reliability. Driving has very demanding safety requirements, and you still need to validate the system in that particular setting. So I see generalist capabilities as something that could make specialized systems easier to build, while specialization remains valuable where performance, cost, and reliability really matter.

r001.rationale: The response says a general-purpose robot does not automatically make an autonomous car obsolete, but does not suggest that owning a driving-capable robot would remove the need to pay extra for autonomous-driving capability in a car.

r002.rationale: The response predicts that generalist robots and specialized systems will coexist and says specialization remains valuable; it does not predict that many specialized systems will struggle to survive.
